display_text:
Teacher. Hwæt sægst ðū, mangere?
Merchant. Ic sęcge ðæt behēfe ic eom ge cyninge and ealdormannum, and weligum, and eallum folce.
Teacher. And hū?
Merchant. Ic āstīge mīn scip mid hlæstum mīnum, and rōwe ofer sǣlice dǣlas, and cīepe mīn ðing, and bycge ðing dēorwierðu, ðā on ðissum lande ne bēoð ācęnnede, and ic hit tōgelǣde ēow hider mid miclum plihte ofer sǣ, and hwīlum forlidennesse ic ðolie, mid lyre ealra ðinga mīnra, unēaðe cwic ætberstende.

original_notes.text: Lat. mercator. Other Old English terms for merchant are cīepa and cīepmann. From a collateral form of the latter, cēapmann, without umlaut, is derived Mod. Eng. chapman. How is chap- related to cheap? See the New English Dictionary (New Eng. Dict.) under these words.
Lat. utilis. Cf. the Mod. Eng. noun behoof.

Carlyle (Sartor Resartus, Bk. 3, Chap. 7) has the following: “König (King), anciently Könning, means Ken-ning (Cunning), or which is the same thing, Can-ning. Ever must the Sovereign of Mankind be fitly entitled King.” On the other hand Gummere (Germanic Origins, p. 270): “At the head of the family we found, of course, the father; and at the head of the state we naturally look for the king. The word ‘king’ means the child or son of the tribe, its representative or even creation; man of race, man of rank. Gradually the king ceases to be regarded as a creation of his race; his ancestry is pushed back to the gods, and his right is quite above all sanctions of popular choice or approval.” Which of these views is confirmed by etymology?
Lat. periculo. Mod. Eng. form of pliht?
Lat. vix vivus evadens. Note the love for alliteration, even in the Latin.
